summary.text: A 61-year-old woman with bipolar disorder presented with disorientation, disorganized speech and behavior, persecutory delusions, verbigeration, agitation and reduced oral intake that progressively worsened over 14 days; she had a catatonic episode one year earlier that resolved with lorazepam, since tapered. Admission laboratory tests, CT and MRI showed no infectious or neurological abnormalities (done to rule out delirium); initial BFCRS was 10.

Because lorazepam was unavailable, oral diazepam 20 mg/day was added to lamotrigine 300 mg/day; BFCRS fell to 2 within 24 hours and 0 within 48 hours. Clozapine was started for mood symptoms, mild sedation led to gradual diazepam tapering, and she was discharged on day 19 in remission of catatonic and mood symptoms on lamotrigine 300 mg/day and clozapine 25 mg/day.

In outpatient follow-up she developed a depressive episode with psychotic features (nihilistic delusions, stereotypy, verbigeration); diazepam 20 mg/day plus venlafaxine was started, catatonic symptoms resolved first then depressive symptoms remitted, and diazepam 5 mg/day was added to maintenance for recurrence of catatonic symptoms.

After three months she developed pneumonia requiring ICU admission, during which all psychiatric medications were tapered and discontinued. Two weeks later she presented to the emergency department with decreased motor activity and verbalization, reduced oral intake, stereotypic movement and fixed gaze (BFCRS 17), was transferred to the inpatient clinic and given diazepam 20 mg/day; BFCRS was 10 within 24 hours and 0 by 48 hours, clozapine, lamotrigine and venlafaxine were reinstated, and she was discharged on hospital day 4.

summary.text: A 62-year-old woman with a history of bipolar disorder (first psychiatric admission at 36 for manic symptoms, five further inpatient admissions for manic episodes, most recent hospitalization eight months before) had been in remission on clozapine 100 mg/day and lithium 600 mg/day until lithium intoxication requiring emergency dialysis one month before admission, after which lithium was stopped and clozapine monotherapy continued.

She was admitted with a 10-day history of progressively worsening mutism, reduced oral intake and psychomotor retardation; BFCRS was 16, indicating severe catatonia. In the absence of lorazepam, oral diazepam 5 mg gave marked improvement within one hour (BFCRS 3); titration to 20 mg/day led to complete resolution (BFCRS 0) within 72 hours.

After catatonia resolved she had depressive symptoms and lithium was cautiously reinitiated with clozapine and diazepam. On hospital day 18 she developed acute respiratory failure secondary to aspiration pneumonia and moved to the ICU, where diazepam and clozapine were gradually tapered; after three days she returned to the psychiatric unit, clozapine and lithium were reintroduced, and she was discharged on day 28 stable without residual catatonic or mood symptoms.

source_coverage.note: Shared statements for both cases (two female patients with bipolar disorder and catatonia treated with oral diazepam; DSM-5 diagnosis and BFCRS monitoring in both cases; remission within 48 to 72 hours pooled). Remainder is background on lorazepam and benzodiazepine literature. The pooled 48-72 hour sentence is attached as supporting evidence to each index-episode recovery outcome; case-specific timings come from b00003/b00004.
Case 1 narrative: three catatonic episodes treated with oral diazepam.
Discussion and literature interpretation; reasoning about diazepam pharmacology and the first case is author opinion, not patient facts; cited studies are not index patients.
Conclusion, ethics approval and consent for publication from both patients: administrative, not clinical facts; case series generalizability limit noted.

article_limitations: Article has no figures or supplements; no visual work applicable.
DSM-5 diagnosis and BFCRS monitoring are stated for "both cases" without specifying every episode of patient 1.
Several time anchors (for example "After three months", "within 72 hours") are not explicit in the source and are preserved as written without calendar dates.
Medication doses for reinstated or reintroduced drugs, and discharge medications for patient 2 and for the second discharge of patient 1, are not stated.
Case series: ethics approval and consent for publication are administrative and not recorded as clinical facts.
The pooled statement "within 48 to 72 hours of initiating oral diazepam" is used only as supporting evidence (index-episode recovery and the patient 2 anchor), never as an individual timing.
